title: Spin singlets are useful
authors: Silas Hoffman, Edward H. Chen, Matthew Brooks, Stephen Carr, Daniel Volya, Alan Tran, Tyler Keating, Thaddeus D. Ladd, Charles Tahan
abstract: We evaluate the utility of the spin-zero manifold of an exchange-coupled array of $N$ spins for tasks in quantum computation and quantum simulation. Since pairs of electrons can be readily initialized into a product state of singlets in semiconducting quantum dot arrays, the full spin-zero manifold is available with exchange-only control, providing a Hilbert space of approximate dimension $2^N/(N/2)^{3/2}$, asymptotically close to the $2^N$ dimension of the full spin Hilbert space. Leveraging the spin-zero manifold enables larger computational space in a given array compared to traditional exchange-only control, in which spin arrays are organized into modular units of $n$ spins comprising $N/n$ encoded qubits, limiting to the exponentially smaller Hilbert dimension $2^{N/n}$. Here we focus on benchmarking metrics for this resource utilization by generalizing cross-entropy benchmarking, mirror benchmarking, and out-of-time-ordered correlators to this system. We show that operating in the spin-zero manifold can accelerate the realization of computational quantum advantage applications in semiconductor-based spin qubits.
summary: This paper demonstrates that restricting the dynamics of an exchange-coupled spin array to its total spin-zero manifold ($	ext{S}_0$) provides a computationally advantageous subspace compared to standard encoding methods. By adapting advanced quantum benchmarks like XEB and OTOCs, the authors show that this physical constraint can accelerate the path toward demonstrating quantum advantage using semiconductor spin qubits.
main_problem: The paper evaluates how utilizing the spin-zero manifold ($	ext{S}_0$) of an exchange-coupled spin array can enhance computational space for quantum simulation and computation beyond limitations imposed by traditional modular qubit encoding.
main_result: Operating within the $	ext{S}_0$ manifold allows for a significantly larger accessible Hilbert space compared to standard methods, and benchmarking metrics like XEB and OTOCs confirm that this subspace supports realizing deep circuits necessary for quantum advantage demonstrations in semiconductor spin qubits.
method: The authors generalize established quantum benchmarking techniques—Cross-Entropy Benchmarking (XEB), Mirror Randomized Benchmarking (MRB), and Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators (OTOCs)—to the specific constraints of the total spin-zero subspace dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using an array of $N$ electron spins in semiconducting quantum dots, governed by Heisenberg exchange interactions. The focus is restricted to the $	ext{S}_0$ manifold, which preserves the total spin zero state exactly.
key_observables: Coarse-grained measurement probabilities ($p_s$), XEB fidelity ($F$), MRB fidelity ($F_{	ext{MRB}}$), and Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators ($	ext{OTOC}_k$).
important_parameters: System size $N$, noise variance $\sigma^2$ (for error scaling), and the ratio of coupling strengths ($\phi = J_2/J_1$) for lattice structures.
main_assumptions: The analysis proceeds despite the coarse-grained nature of readout measurements (Pauli Spin Blockade) and assumes that local error correction can be addressed within the highly entangled $	ext{S}_0$ states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spin array layout, the construction of basis states in the fusion-tree basis for the $	ext{S}_0$ manifold, and simulated probability distributions showing how readout measurements follow an Erlang distribution rather than a standard Porter–Thomas distribution.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical utility of the $	ext{S}_0$ manifold over modular encoding. It then details the generalization of benchmarking metrics (XEB, MRB) to this subspace, providing theoretical predictions based on Beta distributions for measurement probabilities. Finally, it extends the analysis using OTOCs to probe complex dynamics and potential quantum advantage.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges solid-state physics (quantum dots/spins) with advanced quantum information protocols by showing how inherent physical symmetries ($	ext{S}_0$) can be leveraged as a computational resource, providing concrete benchmarking tools for realizing fault-tolerant computation in spin arrays.
